english.html: in the number and catalogue of the smallest and least crimes <sup class="mk" data-key="z">z</sup>. And although St Clement, successor of St Peter (or, according to others, fourth Bishop of Rome), had taught them that after heresy there was no offence more horrible and displeasing to God, nor which deserved to be more sharply and rigorously punished <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>: nevertheless they, having put this crime in the number of the light ones, have willed that for adultery a clerk cannot be degraded, or actually stripped of his sacred orders <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>; for this penalty, they say, is peculiarly reserved for great, enormous and execrable crimes <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>. But in what rank shall we be able to put our Frenchmen? who (if the testimony of Jean Faure and Guillaume Benedicti is believed) long ago put adultery in the number of ingenious and highly praised acts: so far were they from repressing or punishing it <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. Which, by the frequent and multiplied judgments of our company, we have long since made everyone touch with the finger and know to be false, and to have been by them too inconsiderately, and with no little scandal, written and asserted. For if it were so, as they write (which however I could not persuade myself), that for some time lechery had been so far winked at in France that, instead of punishing it and holding it in horror, and especially adultery, some praise was given to it: what more certain argument could we have for esteeming that the judges of that age deserved the title of Barbarians, or of Turks (licensed by their law to every dissoluteness), rather than of Christians? and that they had no light of the knowledge of God, nor of his word? by which we are first taught that our members are members of Jesus Christ, which must not be made members of a harlot, nor soiled by lechery, nor any passion of carnal concupiscence, but possessed in honour and sanctification <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. And afterwards, that lechers and adulterers have always been severely pursued by God, not only by the old law, which condemned them to death <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup> irremissibly, and, as Saint Gregory expounds, without any mercy <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>; but also by the new

notes.citation: Decretals of Gregory IX, title De iudiciis (X 2.1), c. At si clerici (X 2.1.4, Alexander III), § 1
notes.original: c. at ſi cleri. ci. P. i. de iud,⟨alt:iud.⟩
notes.gloss: Clerks accused of lesser crimes — adultery, theft, perjury among them — are judged by the ecclesiastical judge; Coras's "catalogue of the smallest crimes".

notes.citation: Pseudo-Clement, first Epistle to James (the Epistola Clementis ad Iacobum); Decretum of Gratian, Part II, C. 32 q. 7, c. 16 Quid in omnibus (the print's xxx. q. v. is wrong)
notes.original: S. Clemen. en l'epiſtre i. qu'il eſcrit à S. Iaques l'apoſtre c. quid in omnibus. xxx. q. v.
notes.gloss: That after heresy no sin is graver than adultery.

notes.citation: X 2.1, c. Cum non ab homine (X 2.1.10, Alexander III); Panormitanus (Panorme) on it, at the beginning, n. 38
notes.original: cũ non ab homine. de iudic,⟨alt:dic.⟩ Panorme au commencement nu. 38
notes.gloss: A clerk convicted of adultery or like crimes is not to be deposed from his orders but suspended and otherwise punished.

notes.citation: Decretals, title De poenis, c. Tuae discretionis (X 5.37.6, Innocent III; Coras's Tua); and the commentators on the chapters At si clerici and Cum non ab homine just cited
notes.original: c. tua. de pœ. Les Interpretes aux cc. At ſi clerici & cũ non ab homine. alleguez.

notes.citation: Jean Faure (Johannes Faber, d. c. 1340) on Code 8.52 (Quae sit longa consuetudo), l. 1; Guillaume Benedicti (d. 1516), Repetitio on c. Raynutius (Decretals, De testamentis, X 3.26.16), at the words Cuidam Petro, n. 62
notes.original: Iean Faure en la l. i. C. que ſit long,⟨alt:long.⟩ conſ. Guil. Bened. au c. Ray nutius verſic. Cuidam Petro lxij. de teſt.
notes.gloss: Both report that in France adultery went unpunished, which Coras denies from the practice of the Parlement of Toulouse.

notes.citation: 1 Corinthians 6 (6:15–20); 1 Thessalonians 4 (4:3–7) — the print's "second" epistle, chapter iij⟨alt:iiij⟩
notes.original: La premiere des Corinthiẽs c. vi. La ſecon des Teſſalo. c. iij.⟨alt:iiij.⟩
notes.gloss: Our members are members of Christ, not of a harlot; each to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour.

notes.original: Leuitique c,⟨alt:c.⟩ xx. Deuteronome c xxij.

notes.citation: Decretum of Gratian, Part II, C. 23 q. 5, c. 7 Reos [sanguinis] (attributed to Gregory), with Gratian's dictum after it
notes.gloss: For the death penalty of the old law executed without mercy.

readings.reason: annot-083 note z: the same chapter is cited at annot-110 note a as *c. at ſi cleric. de iud.* with a point; a comma closing a marginal note is otherwise unexampled.
annot-083 note d: the same Code title is cited at annot-060 note m as *C. quæ ſit long. conſue.* with a point after *long*.
the passage cited (our members possessed in honour and sanctification) is 1 Thessalonians 4:3-7, chapter iiij; the print's 'seconde' is itself an error, 2 Thessalonians having only three chapters
annot-083 note f: notes e and r of the same annotation read *Leuitique c. xx.* with the point.
xxiij: Causa 23 has a quaestio v; Causa 24 of the Decretum has only three quaestiones
